concept.name: Settlement risk
concept.definition: The risk that one party delivers its side of a transaction but does not receive the countervalue in return — most acutely principal risk in foreign exchange, where the two legs settle in different currencies and time zones. Also called Herstatt risk after the 1974 Bankhaus Herstatt failure.
concept.intuition: You pay out your currency in the morning and the counterparty fails before paying theirs in the afternoon: the whole principal, not just the P/L, is gone.
concept.mechanics: It arises because settlement of the two legs is not simultaneous; it is mitigated by payment-versus-payment (PvP) settlement through financial market infrastructures such as CLS, by netting, and by collateralizing mark-to-market exposure on physically settling FX forwards and swaps. BCBS guidance directs banks to manage principal risk, replacement cost risk, and related liquidity, operational, and legal risks.
concept.formula: Principal exposure = full face value of the currency delivered, outstanding from the time the own-side payment becomes irrevocable until receipt of the countervalue is final.
concept.failure_modes: PvP coverage is incomplete — many currency pairs and jurisdictions settle without it — and netting reduces but does not eliminate principal exposure; settlement failures cluster on stressed days when operational capacity is strained.
concept.misconceptions: Settlement risk is not merely an operational nuisance: the exposure is the full principal for hours at a time, dwarfing the trade's market risk, and it persists even with apparently solvent counterparties because failure can occur intra-day.
concept.example: A bank pays out EUR against USD to a counterparty that is declared insolvent between the EUR payment cut-off and the USD payment time, losing the entire EUR principal.

citations.source: BCBS: Supervisory guidance for managing risks associated with the settlement of foreign exchange transactions
